newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Donors urge more efficient Bangladesh power sector.
newsitem.headline: Donors urge more efficient Bangladesh power sector.

text.p: International donors on Thursday asked Bangladesh to raise efficiency in electricity generation and distribution, sectors dogged by theft and mismanagement.

"They asked for a reduction in losses in power distribution and an improvement in financial management," an Energy Ministry official told Reuters at the end of a four-day donors' meeting to review Bangladesh's energy sector.

Major financiers to Bangladesh's energy sector -- Japan, Britain, Germany, Norway, Asian Development Bank (ADB) and the World Bank -- sat for the review, which will look at a possible withdrawal of a four-year freeze on aid to the sector.
Energy Ministry officials said theft in the power distribution system and the government's reluctance to open electricity generation to the private sector led to the freeze about four years ago.
But Bangladesh's move to liberalise the power and gas sector recently softened donors' stance.
Officials said the meeting might lead to the lifting of the freeze, which has badly affected the power sector.
Sources on the donors' side have indicated, however, they increasingly favour channeling funds through the private sector rather than directly giving it to the government.
The government still controls power generation and distribution in Bangladesh.
Electricity theft costs the exchequer three billion taka ($61 million) each year, according to official figures.
Bangladesh has opened up electricity generation to the private sector, drawing interest from more than a dozen international companies.

Energy Minister Nooruddin Khan told the donors meeting on Monday that Bangladesh would require 185 billion taka ($4.2 bln) worth of investment over the next five years to raise power generation capacity.
Khan said Bangladesh had targeted raising electricity generation to 3,100 megawatts by the year 2,000 and to 4,600 megawatts by 2005 from the current level of 1,850 megawatts.
